title: The Illiterate Who Set Up For a Schoolmaster (മലയാളം)

keywords: the illiterate who set up for a schoolmaster
full_text:
An unemployed laborer in a remote mountain village in Syria noticed that the local school had been closed since the death of the old teacher. Desiring to earn an easy living without turning the heavy spade, the clever fellow purchased an enormous pair of silver spectacles, donned an imposing turban of scholar’s muslin, carried a thick manuscript of ancient parchment under his arm, and opened a schoolroom in the public square.

The villagers, illiterate themselves, marveled at his dignified appearance and entrusted thirty children to his care, paying him with bread, honey, and silver coins.

The fake teacher had a simple system: he distributed wooden slates, had the children copy arbitrary squiggles on the boards, and spent his days smoking his clay pipe and nodding with solemn authority.

One morning, an old peasant woman received a letter from her son who was a soldier in Baghdad. Unable to read, she rushed to the schoolroom, handed the letter to the master, and wept: 'O learned master, read me what my beloved son has written!'

The impostor took the letter, opened it, and stared at the Arabic script in absolute panic—for he could not read a single letter of the alphabet!

Holding the paper before his nose, he began to beat his breast, wail aloud, and tear his turban, shedding dramatic tears!

The poor mother shrieked in terror: 'Alas! Is my son dead? Has he fallen in battle?'

The impostor wept louder, nodding mournfully.

At that moment, the village magistrate, who was a literate scholar, entered the room. Seeing the woman weeping, he took the letter from the schoolmaster’s hands.

The magistrate looked at the letter, and then at the schoolmaster with a sarcastic smile: 'Woman, your son is in splendid health; he has been promoted to captain and has sent you fifty gold dinars with the royal courier! But tell me, master: why were you holding the letter upside down, and why did you invent his death?'

The exposed charlatan fell to his knees, confessing his fraud amidst the laughter and fury of the villagers. He was driven from the village, having learned that true teaching requires real knowledge, not an oversized turban and silver spectacles.
moral: Deceitful pretension in teaching will inevitably be exposed by the simplest test of truth. [ML]
